clinicalPearls: A rare disorder marked by strikingly accelerated osseous (bone) maturation from early infancy despite failure to thrive
Respiratory compromise from a small, unstable upper airway (choanal atresia, laryngomalacia, glossoptosis) is the leading cause of morbidity
Facial features include a prominent forehead, proptosis with shallow orbits, a depressed nasal bridge and micrognathia
Developmental impairment is usually severe, with hypotonia and later kyphoscoliosis
Caused by de novo heterozygous variants in NFIX, a transcription factor of the nuclear factor I family regulating skeletal and neural development
Distinct NFIX variants cause Malan (Sotos-like overgrowth) syndrome, so the same gene produces two contrasting phenotypes
Advanced bone age with poor somatic growth is a paradoxical and characteristic clue
reference.pathophysiology: NFIX encodes a nuclear factor I transcription factor that regulates the expression of genes controlling the proliferation and differentiation of skeletal and neural progenitor cells during development. In Marshall-Smith syndrome, specific variants (often affecting one region of the gene) are thought to escape the normal degradation of aberrant transcripts and exert a dominant effect, dysregulating skeletal maturation and neural development. This produces the paradoxical combination of markedly advanced bone age with poor growth, together with severe developmental impairment and craniofacial and airway anomalies. Different NFIX variants that cause loss of function instead produce the overgrowth-type Malan syndrome, illustrating variant-specific mechanisms.
additionalDifferentials: Other syndromes with advanced bone age
additionalInvestigations: Bone-age radiograph and skeletal survey demonstrating advanced maturation
Airway evaluation including endoscopy for laryngomalacia and choanal patency
Targeted NFIX sequencing or a gene panel or exome sequencing
redFlags: Upper airway obstruction and respiratory failure
reference.prognosis: Marshall-Smith syndrome carries a guarded prognosis, with early mortality historically driven by airway and respiratory complications; survivors have severe developmental impairment. Proactive airway and respiratory management can improve survival, and care is supportive and multidisciplinary.
pitfalls: Underestimating the airway risk and its impact on survival
Confusing it with the overgrowth-type Malan syndrome caused by other NFIX variants
Mislabelling advanced bone age as an overgrowth disorder despite poor somatic growth
Delaying respiratory assessment in an infant with failure to thrive
management: No disease-specific therapy; care is supportive and centred on securing the airway
Proactive upper-airway management for choanal atresia, laryngomalacia and glossoptosis, including choanal surgery, CPAP or tracheostomy where needed
Respiratory support and treatment of recurrent respiratory infections, with surveillance for sleep-disordered breathing
Nutritional support for failure to thrive, including gastrostomy feeding where oral intake is inadequate
Early developmental support and therapies for the severe developmental impairment and hypotonia
Orthopaedic monitoring and management of kyphoscoliosis
Usually de novo: offer genetic counselling with parental testing, as recurrence risk is generally low
Coordinate care through a multidisciplinary team including ENT, respiratory, genetics and developmental paediatrics
